title: Trusted Relationship
summary: Trusted relationship abuse means an adversary enters through a third party that already holds legitimate access to the target, rather than attacking the target's own perimeter. Managed service providers, IT contractors, cloud resellers and infrastructure vendors are typically given remote management channels, service accounts, or delegated administrative roles, and that access is often excluded from the strictest controls because it is needed for support work. Compromising the provider, or simply using a stolen provider credential, gives the adversary a path that terminates inside the victim environment with a valid account. In cloud tenants the same idea appears as delegated administrator relationships, where a compromised partner account can be leveraged to control a customer tenant or to send new delegation offers. The telemetry looks like a successful login from a support account at an unusual hour, from an unexpected country, or reaching systems outside the vendor's stated scope, so baselining which provider identities normally touch which resources is what separates abuse from routine maintenance.

beginner.definition: This is when an attacker does not break into your company directly. Instead, they get in through a supplier or partner who already has access to you. That partner may be an IT support firm, a security company or a building systems contractor. The attacker uses the partner's account as a door key.
beginner.whyItMatters: Your security checks do not see this as an attack, because the login looks like a real partner. These partners often hold powerful access so they can fix things quickly. Their own security may be weaker than yours, and that becomes your risk. The attacker can reach many systems before anyone suspects the supplier.
howItWorks: You give a third party access to manage part of your network or cloud account.
The attacker targets that third party, often because smaller suppliers have weaker defences.
The attacker steals or reuses a provider account, a token or a remote support tool session.
They log in through the trusted channel and appear as a normal supplier user.
In cloud services they may use delegated administrator rights, or send a new delegation offer to a customer.
The access is then used to reach internal systems, create accounts or move toward data.
beginner.example: Imagine a hospital night desk. An outside maintenance company has a master key so its staff can fix the lifts at any hour. A thief copies that key from the maintenance office and walks in through the staff entrance. The desk clerk sees a familiar uniform and a valid key, so nobody asks questions. The only oddity is that a lift engineer is opening a records room.
takeaways: Third party access must be reviewed often, and removed as soon as the work ends.
Watch vendor logins for odd hours, odd locations and systems outside their agreed scope.
A partner breach is your breach, so ask suppliers how they protect their own accounts.

objectives: Explain how access through a trusted third party differs from attacking an organisation directly.
Identify common third parties that hold elevated or remote access, such as IT and managed service providers.
Describe how delegated administrator relationships in cloud tenants can be abused.
Recognise authentication and audit records that reveal provider account misuse.
Describe controls such as scoped access, time limits and periodic reviews of third party accounts.
